title: Better data, better policies, better outcomes for kids and safety
summary: Youth crime has been on a steady decline, but you might not know it to read the headlines, writes Robin Campbell, who blames it on a lack of solid data, and calls for state agencies to work together to streamline data and help the public understand.
content:
by Robin Campbell, Maryland Matters January 2, 2026

by Robin Campbell, Maryland Matters January 2, 2026

Even as Baltimore celebrates a historic drop in homicides, everyone seems to have a different opinion about whether crime by the city’s young people is falling, rising, changing, or staying the same. When those opinions are based on a personal experience of harm, they deserve compassion and support. When they are not, it is reasonable to ask, What evidence are we drawing from?

With support from the Abell Foundation, I have been tracking available youth justice data to fact-check commonly heard claims about Baltimore crime involving young people and to gauge how the system is responding.

Here are some of the things I found: Youth offending has mostly continued its long decline in Baltimore, as it has nationally; the COVID-19 pandemic was a tremendous disruptor that made at least three years — 2020, 2021 and 2022 — unreliable outliers in almost any extended trend analysis; and the youth justice system, in Baltimore and statewide, deserves a lot more informed scrutiny.

Arrest data is a widely accepted, if imperfect, measure of youth offending. Recently published studies show that arrests of young people in Baltimore and across the nation have been trending down for many years, took a deep dive during the COVID-19 pandemic, and began recovering to pre-pandemic levels around 2023. The most reliable long-term data for Baltimore, from the state’s Department of Juvenile Services (DJS), shows that FY 2019 was the last year of a steady decline prior to the appearance of COVID-19, with 1,387 “complaints”—incidents reported to the agency by police and other sources. By FY 2021, when the pandemic was having its greatest impact, DJS received just 582 complaints. The numbers have rebounded since then, to 1,768 in FY 2025, but they are still well below levels recorded prior to FY 2019.

A corollary to widespread concerns about youth offending are frequently heard complaints about how the justice system is holding Baltimore young people accountable for crimes they may have committed. Once again, the evidence is not what media headlines might lead us to believe; in some ways the data suggest we are being too tough.

Maryland’s practice of automatically sending some arrested youth directly into the adult criminal justice system based on charges from police and prosecutors is one example. This practice — which Maryland does more than nearly every other state — has youths 17 and younger facing adult sentences and, if convicted, possible time in adult facilities.

Yet data published online by the Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Protection (GOCPP) shows that since FY 2021 the most common autocharge offense statewide has been illegal gun possession. According to data shared directly by GOCPP,  in Baltimore illegal gun charges have been the most common autocharge offense since at least FY 2019. In FY 2024 they accounted for nearly half — 45% — of all such charges in the city.

No one disputes that kids and illegal guns are an awful combination that demands serious attention and action. But research has shown that most youth who arm themselves do so because they are afraid, not because they want to hurt someone.

New interventions like DJS’ Thrive Academy and the city’s Group Violence Reduction Strategy suggest there may be better ways to allay these fears than months of pretrial detention and threats of time in an adult prison — which, in addition to being expensive, are known to increase the risk of recidivism and result in poor long-term outcomes, such as lost education, reduced job opportunities and compromised health.

Among the most important findings, however, is that agencies within the juvenile justice system could do a better job working together to help the public understand aggregate data about system-involved kids. DJS publishes a vast amount of information once a year about youth in its care. But this agency represents only a portion of the juvenile justice system.

At the very least, data from all of the relevant agencies, including the state’s Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, could be made more compatible. As it is, seemingly interchangeable categories tracked by different agencies — like “arrests,” “complaints,” “charges” and “cases” — mask crucial distinctions that make cross-agency comparisons difficult, if not impossible.

Baltimore’s young people are associated with less than 10% of the city’s crime. Yet when it comes to talk about community safety, our kids are front and center. Making youth justice data more accessible and better understood could keep public opinion from being disproportionately shaped by rumor, algorithms and media headlines about individual incidents. The result could be policy solutions that are better for kids, communities, and limited state budgets alike.
